meta.title: Finding Similar Items at Scale — Part 2
meta.subtitle: Shingling, Jaccard similarity and minhash signatures
meta.summary: To find similar items without comparing them whole, see every entity as a set: shingle documents into k-grams, compare the sets with Jaccard similarity, and compress each set into a short minhash signature that preserves that similarity in expectation — computed in one pass with row hashing.
objectives: Explain why finding similar items is reduced to finding similar sets, and list the applications of set similarity.
Compute the Jaccard similarity of sets and of bags.
Shingle a document into k-shingles, choose k, and explain hashed and word-based shingles.
Represent sets as columns of a boolean matrix and classify its rows into types a, b, c and d.
Compute minhash values from row permutations and explain why P[h(C₁) = h(C₂)] = SIM(C₁, C₂).
Build a signature matrix in one pass with row hashing, and estimate similarity from signatures.
Explain how minhashing over only the first m rows speeds things up, and how ∞ values are counted.
takeaways: Too many entities cost time and too large entities cost space: see entities as sets and reduce finding similar items to finding similar sets.

Set similarity drives near-duplicate detection, plagiarism, mirror pages, news aggregation and collaborative filtering; bag similarity counts each element min-times in the intersection and sum-times in the union.
A document is represented by its set of k-shingles; k must make any given shingle unlikely in any given document (5 for short documents, about 9–10 for long ones).
Hashing 9-shingles to four bytes discriminates better than using 4-shingles; shingles built from stop words favour the news article over the page clutter.
In the boolean matrix SIM(C₁, C₂) = a / (a + b + c): only rows with a 1 in at least one column count.
The minhash of a column is the first row, in a random permutation, with a 1 — and P[h(C₁) = h(C₂)] = SIM(C₁, C₂).
Signature similarity is the fraction of minhash functions that agree; its expected value is the Jaccard similarity, and longer signatures shrink the error.
Row hashing replaces permutations: one slot per column and hash function, initialised to ∞, lowered whenever a row with a 1 hashes below it.

concepts.short: Many data-mining problems reduce to finding sets with a large intersection relative to their union.
concepts.detail: Entity resolution, pages with similar words (topic classification, plagiarism, repetition avoidance), customers with similar purchases or users with similar tastes in movies (recommendation), and the dual — movies with similar sets of fans. The similarity is textual or set-based, not similarity of meaning.

concepts.short: Count an element min(times in B, times in C) in the intersection and the sum of its counts in the union.
concepts.detail: Used when ratings become repeated elements (a movie rated n stars appears n times). With this definition the maximum is 1/2: {a, a, a, b} and {a, a, b, b, c} have intersection 3 and union 9, similarity 1/3.

concepts.short: The set of all length-k substrings (or word sequences, or any tokens) occurring in a document.
concepts.detail: Shingling turns lexical similarity into set overlap and survives reordering: changing a word only affects shingles within distance $k$ of it, and moving a paragraph only changes the $2k$ shingles that cross its boundaries. Pick $k$ large enough that any given shingle is unlikely in any given document.

concepts.short: Represent a document by the set of hash values of its k-shingles.
concepts.detail: Hashing 9-shingles down to 32 bits discriminates better than using 4-shingles directly, even though both cost four bytes: only about $20^4 = 160{,}000$ 4-shingles actually occur in English text, while hashed 9-shingles use the whole 32-bit range. Two documents can rarely appear to share a shingle when only the hash values collided.

concepts.short: A stop word followed by the next two words — tuned for finding the same news article on different pages.
concepts.detail: News prose is full of stop words, ads and navigation are not. Shingles anchored on stop words therefore come mostly from the article, so pages with the same article and different surroundings score higher than pages with the same surroundings and a different article.

concepts.term: Jaccard similarity and the row types
concepts.short: SIM(C₁, C₂) = |C₁ ∩ C₂| / |C₁ ∪ C₂| = a / (a + b + c).
concepts.detail: Classify the rows of two columns as type a (1, 1), b (1, 0), c (0, 1) or d (0, 0). Intersection counts type a, union counts types a, b and c — type-d rows, the vast majority in a sparse matrix, never matter.

concepts.short: Rows are elements of the universal set, columns are sets, a 1 means membership.
concepts.detail: Encoding sets as 0/1 vectors turns intersection into bitwise AND and union into bitwise OR. The matrix is almost always extremely sparse, so it is a way of thinking rather than a storage format.

concepts.short: Permute the rows; the minhash of a column is the number of the first row in which it has a 1.
concepts.detail: The surprising property is $P[h(C_1) = h(C_2)] = SIM(C_1, C_2)$: looking down the permuted columns until the first 1 appears, the hashes agree exactly when that row is type a, so the probability is $a/(a+b+c)$.

concepts.short: One short column of minhash values per set, one row per minhash function.
concepts.detail: The similarity of two signatures is the fraction of minhash functions (rows) in which they agree. Its expected value equals the Jaccard similarity of the underlying sets, and the longer the signatures, the smaller the expected error; 100 functions is typical.

concepts.short: Simulate random permutations with hash functions in a single pass over the rows.
concepts.detail: Permuting a billion rows even once is prohibitive, storing the permutation takes a billion entries, and reading rows in permuted order thrashes. Instead keep a slot per column and hash function initialised to ∞, scan the rows once, and lower the slot whenever a row with a 1 hashes below the current value.

concepts.term: Minhashing on the first m rows
concepts.short: Compute each minhash from only m of the k rows, accepting an occasional ∞.
concepts.detail: Work drops by a factor k/m. A row where one column is ∞ and the other is not counts as a disagreement; a row where both are ∞ carries no information and is ignored. Splitting the rows into k/m groups yields k/m minhash values from one hash function and one pass, and balances out the estimation error.

quiz.prompt: Entity identification is based on similarity. What goes wrong when there are too many entities, or they are too large — and what is the approach?

options.text: Too many comparisons (time) and too much memory (space); see entities as sets and look for similar sets.
The similarity measures stop being distance measures; switch to Euclidean distance.
Nothing — a faster machine solves it.
Entities can no longer be hashed; use B+ trees instead.

quiz.explanation: Comparing everything costs time, and large entities cost space. Representing each entity as a **set** reduces finding similar items to finding similar sets, which shingling, minhashing and LSH then make cheap.

quiz.prompt: What is the Jaccard similarity of the bags {a, a, a, b} and {a, a, b, b, c}?
quiz.explanation: The intersection counts *a* twice (the minimum of 3 and 2) and *b* once: size 3. The bag union is the sum of the sizes, 4 + 5 = 9. So the similarity is $3/9 = 1/3$ — and since the maximum for bags is 1/2, that is quite similar.

quiz.prompt: What does representing a document by its k-shingles give you that a set of important words does not?

options.text: It makes the representation smaller than the document.
It removes the need for a distance measure.
It keeps local word order, so reordering paragraphs changes only the shingles crossing the boundaries.
It guarantees that no two documents share any shingle.

quiz.explanation: Shingles capture short sequences, so order matters locally. Changing one word only affects the shingles within distance $k$ of it, and reordering paragraphs only affects the $2k$ shingles that cross the boundaries. Shingle sets are **larger** than the document, which is exactly why minhashing follows.

quiz.prompt: What goes wrong if you pick the shingle size k too small — say k = 1 on web pages?

options.text: Almost every document contains almost every shingle, so unrelated documents look highly similar.
The shingle sets become too large to hash.
Jaccard similarity becomes negative.
Minhashing can no longer be applied.

quiz.explanation: k must be large enough that any given shingle is unlikely to appear in any given document. With $k = 1$ nearly every page contains nearly every common character. A rule of thumb is $k = 5$ for short documents and $k = 10$ for long ones; the book $k = 5$ for emails and $k = 9$ for research articles.

quiz.prompt: Why do hashed 9-shingles (4 bytes each) discriminate better than plain 4-shingles (also 4 bytes)?

options.text: Hash functions remove stop words.
Only about 20⁴ = 160,000 different 4-shingles are likely in English text, while hashed 9-shingles spread over almost all 2³² values.
9-shingles never collide.
They don't — both carry exactly the same information.

quiz.explanation: Most four-byte sequences never occur in real text, so 4-shingles use a small part of the space. There are many more than $2^{32}$ likely 9-shingles, so after hashing almost any 32-bit value is possible.

quiz.prompt: For two columns of a boolean matrix, which rows determine their Jaccard similarity?

options.text: Only the rows where both columns are 0.
All rows equally.
Rows of types a, b and c; SIM = a / (a + b + c).
Only the rows of type a.

quiz.explanation: Type a (1, 1) rows form the intersection; types a, b (1, 0) and c (0, 1) form the union. Type d (0, 0) rows — most rows of a sparse matrix — never matter.

quiz.prompt: What is the defining property of minhashing?

options.text: It compresses any set to exactly four bytes.
The probability that two columns have the same minhash value equals their Jaccard similarity.
It sorts the rows so that similar columns become adjacent.
It removes every type-d row from the matrix.

quiz.explanation: Looking down the permuted columns until the first 1 appears, the two minhashes agree exactly when that row is type a and disagree on types b and c. So $P[h(C_1) = h(C_2)] = a/(a+b+c) = SIM(C_1, C_2)$.

quiz.prompt: In the running example, columns 1 and 3 have Jaccard similarity 0.75 but their three-row signatures agree in only 2 of 3 rows. What does that show?

options.text: Minhashing is biased and underestimates similarity.
Signature similarity equals the Jaccard similarity only in expectation; short signatures have large errors.
The permutations were chosen wrongly.
Columns 1 and 3 are not similar.

quiz.explanation: The **expected** signature similarity is the Jaccard similarity, but with three minhash functions the estimate is coarse — columns 2 and 4 (also 0.75) happen to agree in all three. Longer signatures shrink the expected error.

quiz.prompt: Why does real minhashing use row hashing instead of random permutations?

options.text: Permutations do not preserve Jaccard similarity.
With a billion rows, picking and storing a random permutation is impractical and reading rows in permuted order thrashes.
Hash functions give exact similarities, permutations only estimates.
Row hashing needs no memory at all.

quiz.explanation: Representing one random permutation of a billion rows takes a billion entries, and accessing rows in permuted order leads to thrashing. Each hash function $k_i$ induces an ordering of the rows that acts as a random permutation, computed in one sequential pass.

quiz.prompt: Minhashing only the first m rows, one minhash value is ∞ for both columns. How is that row of the signatures counted?

options.text: As an agreement — both values are equal.
As a disagreement.
As neither: both columns had only 0s in those m rows, so it carries no information and is ignored.
The whole signature must be recomputed.

quiz.explanation: If only one column is ∞, the other has a 1 among the first m rows while the ∞ column does not, so it is a disagreement. If both are ∞, the similarity depends only on rows we chose not to look at, so the row counts neither way.

blocks.md:
Entity identification is based on similarity — on finding similar items. For a small number of entities of relatively small size, things are manageable. But what if there are **too many** entities? Then there are too many comparisons (**time**). What if the entities are **too large**? Then the memory requirements explode (**space**).

The approach: **see entities as sets**. Finding similar items is then reduced to finding similar sets.

headers: Problem expressed as finding similar sets
rows: Records describing the same real-world entity
Classification by topic, plagiarism, avoiding repetition
Netflix users with similar tastes in movies
Dual: movies with similar sets of fans
blocks.caption: Many data-mining problems can be expressed as finding similar sets.

blocks.md:
**Similarity of documents** (MMDS §3.1.2) is about *character-level* similarity, not similar meaning. Testing for exact duplicates is easy — compare character by character. The interesting cases share large portions of text without being identical:

- **Plagiarism** — the plagiarist may take only parts of a document, alter a few words and reorder sentences.
- **Mirror pages** — popular sites are duplicated on several hosts; each copy differs slightly (host information, links to the *other* mirrors). Course pages reused from year to year behave the same way. Search engines should avoid showing near-identical pages on the first page of results.
- **Articles from the same source** — one news-agency article is republished by many newspapers, each cutting paragraphs, adding material and surrounding it with its own logo, ads and links. Aggregators such as Google News want to show only one version.

**Collaborative filtering** (MMDS §3.1.3) recommends to users what similar users liked. Amazon can call two customers similar when their sets of purchased items have high Jaccard similarity — and two items similar when their sets of buyers do. Here similarities need not be high to be significant: mirror sites may exceed 90%, but even 20% can mark customers with similar tastes. Netflix movie ratings are not binary, so the book offers three ways to turn them into sets: ignore low ratings; give each movie two elements, *liked* and *hated*; or, for 1-to-5 stars, put a movie into a customer's **bag** $n$ times for $n$ stars and use bag similarity.

blocks.caption: Jaccard similarity of bags. With the union defined as the sum of the bag sizes, the largest possible value is 1/2.

blocks.title: The concrete goal
blocks.md: Given a large number $N$ of documents — millions or billions — find the **near-duplicate** pairs. Three problems stand in the way: there are too many documents to compare all pairs; documents are so large or so many that they cannot fit in main memory; and many small pieces of one document can appear **out of order** in another, so order matters.

tasks.prompt: What is the Jaccard similarity of {1, 2, 3, 4} and {2, 4, 6}?
What is the Jaccard bag similarity of {1, 1, 1, 2} and {1, 1, 2, 2, 3}?
tasks.solution: Intersection: 1 counted min(3, 2) = 2 times, 2 counted min(1, 2) = 1 time — size 3. Union: 4 + 5 = 9. Similarity **1/3**.

blocks.md: How do you turn a document into a set? A set of words, or of “important” words, is not effective — it throws away order. **Shingling** keeps it: generate the set of strings of length $k$ that appear in the document. A **k-shingle** (or k-gram) is a sequence of $k$ characters, $k$ words, or $k$ of any other token.

steps.title: Shingle each document
steps.md: $D_1 = abcab$ gives {ab, bc, ca} — *ab* occurs twice but appears once in the set. $D_2 = abfef$ gives {ab, bf, fe, ef}.

steps.title: Fix an order on all shingles
steps.md: The shingles seen are [ab, bc, ca, bf, fe, ef].

steps.title: Each document becomes a 0/1 vector
steps.md: $D_1 = [1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0]$ and $D_2 = [1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]$ — vectors in the space of shingles, and very **sparse** ones in practice. Their Jaccard similarity is $1/6$.

blocks.md:
Documents that are intuitively similar have **many shingles in common**. Changing a word only affects the k-shingles within distance $k$ of that word, and reordering paragraphs only affects the $2k$ shingles that cross paragraph boundaries. With $k = 3$, *The dog which chased the cat* versus *The dog that chased the cat* replaces only seven 3-shingles: `g_w`, `_wh`, `whi`, `hic`, `ich`, `ch_` and `h_c`.

White space deserves care: replace any run of blanks, tabs and newlines by a single blank rather than deleting it, so shingles spanning two words stay distinct. With $k = 9$, *touch down* gives `touch dow` and `ouch down` while *touchdown* gives `touchdown`.

blocks.title: Selecting the right k
blocks.md: Pick $k$ large enough that the probability of any given shingle appearing in any given document is low; with $k = 1$ almost all web pages share almost all characters. A rule of thumb is **$k = 5$ for short documents** and **$k = 10$ for long documents**. The book reasons the same way: for emails, $27^5 \approx 14$ million possible 5-shingles is plenty — though since common letters dominate, imagine only 20 characters and estimate $20^k$ — and **$k = 9$** is considered safe for research articles.

**Hashing shingles.** Represent a document by the set of **hash values** of its k-shingles: for $D_1 = abcab$, $S(D_1) = \{ab, bc, ca\}$ might become $h(D_1) = \{1, 5, 7\}$. Two documents could (rarely) appear to share shingles when in fact only the hash values were shared. The book maps 9-shingles to buckets in $[0, 2^{32} - 1]$, four bytes instead of nine — and this discriminates **better** than 4-shingles, which also cost four bytes: only about $20^4 = 160{,}000$ different 4-shingles are likely in English, while hashed 9-shingles fill almost the whole 32-bit range.

**Selecting the right token** matters too. For finding the same news article on different pages, the book defines a shingle as a **stop word followed by the next two words**. News prose is full of stop words; ads and navigation are not, so the article contributes most of the shingles. *A spokesperson for the Sudzo Corporation revealed today…* yields *A spokesperson for*, *for the Sudzo*, *the Sudzo Corporation* and more; the ad *Buy Sudzo* yields none.

blocks.title: Shingling explorer
blocks.description: Change k, switch between character and word tokens, and watch which shingles two documents actually share.

tasks.prompt: How many distinct 2-shingles does the document *abcdabd* have?
tasks.solution: {ab, bc, cd, da, bd}: **5** — *ab* occurs twice but counts once.

tasks.prompt: What is the largest number of k-shingles a document of n characters can have (assuming the alphabet is large enough)?
tasks.solution: One shingle starts at each of the first **n − k + 1** positions, and in the best case they are all different.

blocks.md:
With documents as sets, similarity is **Jaccard similarity** (Lecture 2): the size of the intersection over the size of the union — two sets sharing 3 elements out of 8 distinct ones have similarity 3/8.

Many similarity problems can be formalised as finding subsets with a significant intersection. **Encode sets as 0/1 vectors**, one dimension per element of the universal set: set intersection becomes **bitwise AND** and union **bitwise OR**. For $C_1 = 10111$ and $C_2 = 10011$ the intersection has size 3 and the union size 4, so the Jaccard *similarity* is 3/4 and the *distance* 1/4.

blocks.title: The challenge
blocks.md: Suppose we need near-duplicate documents among $N = 1$ million documents. Naïvely we compute the Jaccard similarity of every pair: $N(N-1)/2 \approx 5 \times 10^{11}$ comparisons. At $10^5$ seconds per day and $10^6$ comparisons per second, that takes **5 days**. For $N = 10$ million it takes more than a year. The solution: construct much smaller **signatures** of the items and compare those instead.

Picture all the sets together as one **boolean matrix**: **rows** are the elements of the universal set (for example, all k-shingles), **columns** are the sets, and there is a 1 in row $e$ and column $S$ if and only if $e$ is a member of $S$. Column similarity is the Jaccard similarity of the sets of rows in which they have a 1. The typical matrix is very sparse — it is a way of thinking, never actually stored.

blocks.caption: Column similarity: 2 rows in the intersection, 5 in the union, Sim(C₁, C₂) = 2/5 = 0.4.
Given two columns, every row is one of four types. With a = the number of type-a rows, etc., Sim(C₁, C₂) = a / (a + b + c).

cards.prompt: How long does comparing all pairs of 1 million documents take, and what is the way out?
cards.answer: ≈ 5 × 10¹¹ comparisons, about 5 days at 10⁶ per second; compare much smaller signatures instead.

cards.prompt: In the boolean matrix, what are rows, columns and a 1?
cards.answer: Rows are elements of the universal set (e.g. shingles), columns are sets, a 1 means the element belongs to the set.

cards.prompt: Express Jaccard similarity in terms of row types.
cards.answer: a / (a + b + c) — type-d rows (0, 0) don't count.

blocks.md: **Minhashing** converts large sets into short signatures while preserving similarity. Imagine the rows of the boolean matrix **permuted randomly**. The **minhash function** $h(C)$ is the number of the first row, in the permuted order, in which column $C$ has a 1. Use several — e.g. 100 — independent permutations to create a signature for each column. The signatures form another matrix, the **signature matrix**, whose columns represent the sets and whose rows are the minhash values, one per permutation.

blocks.caption: The running example: three permutations (each πᵢ gives a row's position in the permuted order) and a 7 × 4 input matrix of shingles × documents.
The signature matrix M. Under π₁, column C₁ has 1s in rows at positions 2, 3, 5 and 4 — so the 2nd element of the permutation is the first to map to a 1, and h₁(C₁) = 2.

blocks.title: The surprising property
blocks.md:
The probability, over all permutations of the rows, that $h(C_1) = h(C_2)$ is the same as $Sim(C_1, C_2)$. **Both are $a / (a + b + c)$!**

Why? Look down the permuted columns $C_1$ and $C_2$ until you see the first 1. Type-d rows are skipped. If that row is type a, then $h(C_1) = h(C_2)$; if it is type b or c, then not. Every one of the $a + b + c$ rows is equally likely to come first.

The **similarity of signatures** is the fraction of the minhash functions in which they agree — thinking of signatures as columns of integers, the fraction of rows in which they agree. Thus the **expected** similarity of two signatures equals the Jaccard similarity of the sets they represent, and the longer the signatures, the smaller the expected error.

blocks.caption: Signature similarity estimates Jaccard similarity: right on average, noisy with only three minhash functions.

tasks.prompt: In the example, column C₃ has 1s in rows 1, 6 and 7. Under π₂ those rows sit at positions 4, 7 and 5. What is h₂(C₃)?
tasks.solution: The first position, in permuted order, holding a 1 for C₃ is the smallest of 4, 7 and 5: **4**.

tasks.prompt: Signatures [2, 2, 1] and [2, 4, 1] — what is their signature similarity?
tasks.solution: They agree in the first and third minhash: **2/3** — the estimate for C₁–C₃, whose true Jaccard similarity is 0.75.

blocks.md:
Suppose there are **1 billion rows**. It is hard to pick a random permutation of 1…billion; representing one takes 1 billion entries; and accessing rows in permuted order leads to thrashing. Permuting rows even once is prohibitive.

**Row hashing** solves it: pick $K = 100$ hash functions $k_i$; the ordering of the rows under $k_i$ gives a random row permutation. And it can be done in **one pass**: for each column $C$ and hash function $k_i$ keep a *slot* for the minhash value, initialise every $sig(C)[i] = \infty$, and scan the rows looking for 1s. If row $j$ has a 1 in column $C$, then for each $k_i$: if $k_i(j) < sig(C)[i]$, set $sig(C)[i] \leftarrow k_i(j)$.

blocks.caption: The algorithm: one pass over the rows builds every signature at once.

blocks.title: Minhash signature builder
blocks.description: The worked example from the lecture. Step through the rows and watch the signature slots fall from infinity. Click any 0/1 cell to change the input and see what happens.

blocks.title: Hand-trace the lecture example
blocks.intro: Rows 1–5, two columns, $h(x) = x \bmod 5$ and $g(x) = (2x+1) \bmod 5$. Column $C_1$ has 1s in rows 1, 3, 4; column $C_2$ in rows 2, 3, 5.

steps.title: Initialise every slot to infinity
steps.md: $sig(C_1) = [\infty, \infty]$ and $sig(C_2) = [\infty, \infty]$. Nothing has been seen yet.

steps.title: Row 1 — h(1) = 1, g(1) = 3
steps.md: Only $C_1$ has a 1, so $sig(C_1) = [1, 3]$. $C_2$ is untouched.

steps.title: Row 3 — h(3) = 3, g(3) = 2
steps.md: Both columns have a 1. For $C_1$, 3 is not below 1 but 2 is below 3, so $sig(C_1) = [1, 2]$. For $C_2$, neither 3 nor 2 improves on $[2, 0]$.

steps.title: Row 4 — h(4) = 4, g(4) = 4
steps.md: Only $C_1$ has a 1, and neither 4 improves on $[1, 2]$. Nothing changes.

steps.title: Row 5 — h(5) = 0, g(5) = 1
steps.md: Only $C_2$ has a 1. Now $0 < 2$, so the first slot drops: $sig(C_2) = [0, 0]$.

steps.title: Read off the result
steps.md: $sig(C_1) = [1, 2]$ and $sig(C_2) = [0, 0]$ — they agree in zero rows. The true Jaccard similarity is $1/5 = 0.2$: only row 3 is type a, rows 1, 2, 4 and 5 are type b or c. Two hash functions are simply not enough to estimate 0.2; that is the noise 100 hashes average away.

blocks.md:
**Speeding up minhashing** (MMDS §3.3.6–§3.3.7). Each minhash function still examines all $k$ rows. Instead, compute it from only the **first $m$ rows**, cutting the work by a factor $k/m$. A column with only 0s in those rows gets the value $\infty$, and signatures are compared with three cases:

1. Neither column is $\infty$: count agreement or disagreement as usual.
2. One column is $\infty$, the other not: the other column has a 1 among the first $m$ rows and the $\infty$ column does not — count a **disagreement**.
3. Both are $\infty$: the first $m$ rows say nothing about these sets, so count **neither**.

As long as case 3 is rare, accuracy barely suffers, and the time saved buys extra minhash functions. With hash functions instead of true permutations, hash only the first $m$ rows and take the minimum seen so far. Better still, split the $k$ rows into $k/m$ groups and compute one minhash value per group: a single hash function and a single pass yield $k/m$ signature rows, and errors in one group are balanced by the others.

blocks.title: MMDS Example 3.9: two groups of four rows

steps.title: First four rows
steps.md: $S_1$ has no 1 there, so its minhash is $\infty$ and never agrees with $S_2$: restricted to these rows, $SIM(S_1, S_2) = 0$.

steps.title: Last four rows
steps.md: Restricted to rows 5–8, $S_1 = \{5,6,7\}$ and $S_2 = \{5,6\}$, so their similarity there is $2/3$.

steps.title: Expected agreement
steps.md: The two minhash values agree with expected fraction $(0 + 2/3)/2 = 1/3$, against a true 1/2 — an error, but not a large one. For $S_1, S_3$ it is $(0 + 1/3)/2 = 1/6$ against 1/5, and for $S_2, S_3$ exactly 1/2. With far more than four rows per group the expected error approaches zero.

cards.prompt: Why can't you just permute the rows?
cards.answer: With a billion rows, picking and storing a random permutation is impractical (a billion entries), and reading rows in permuted order thrashes.
Slots sig(C)[i] = ∞ for every column and hash function; scan rows; for a row j with a 1 in column C, set sig(C)[i] = kᵢ(j) whenever kᵢ(j) is smaller.

cards.prompt: Minhashing on the first m rows: how is a signature row counted when one column is ∞? When both are?
cards.answer: One ∞: a disagreement. Both ∞: neither — the row is ignored.

blocks.title: Using a set of words instead of shingles
blocks.md: A bag or set of words loses order, so it cannot tell a plagiarised paragraph from the same words used differently. Shingles keep local order.

blocks.title: Choosing k too small
blocks.md: With tiny $k$ every document contains most shingles and everything looks similar. Choose $k$ so that a given shingle is unlikely in a given document.

blocks.title: Deleting white space
blocks.md: Collapse runs of white space into one blank instead of removing it, or *touch down* and *touchdown* become indistinguishable.

blocks.title: Estimating similarity from a short signature
blocks.md: Expected signature similarity equals Jaccard similarity, but with 2 or 3 minhash functions the variance is enormous — the hand-traced example estimates 0.2 as 0.0. Unbiased is not the same as accurate.

blocks.title: Reading the minhash as a row number before permuting
blocks.md: $h(C)$ is the position, **in the permuted order**, of the first row with a 1 — not the original row index. In the running example the permutation columns give exactly those positions.
Ten questions on turning entities into sets and sets into signatures.

items: Too many entities cost time and too large entities cost space: see entities as sets and reduce finding similar items to finding similar sets.

Set similarity drives near-duplicate detection, plagiarism, mirror pages, news aggregation and collaborative filtering; bag similarity counts each element min-times in the intersection and sum-times in the union.
A document is represented by its set of k-shingles; k must make any given shingle unlikely in any given document (5 for short documents, about 9–10 for long ones).
Hashing 9-shingles to four bytes discriminates better than using 4-shingles; shingles built from stop words favour the news article over the page clutter.
In the boolean matrix SIM(C₁, C₂) = a / (a + b + c): only rows with a 1 in at least one column count.
The minhash of a column is the first row, in a random permutation, with a 1 — and P[h(C₁) = h(C₂)] = SIM(C₁, C₂).
Signature similarity is the fraction of minhash functions that agree; its expected value is the Jaccard similarity, and longer signatures shrink the error.
Row hashing replaces permutations: one slot per column and hash function, initialised to ∞, lowered whenever a row with a 1 hashes below it.

rows: Shingle sets are as large as documents
k/m less work using m of k rows

blocks.title: The one sentence version
blocks.md: Turn each document into its set of shingles, and each set into a short minhash signature whose agreement rate with another signature estimates their Jaccard similarity — small enough to fit in memory, but still one comparison per pair, which Part 3 fixes.
